newsitem.title: ITALY: FEATURE - Italy's "mamma's boys" reluctant to leave the nest.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Italy's "mamma's boys" reluctant to leave the nest.

text.p: Alessandro Perone Pacifico is 35, has a degree in electronic engineering, works for Italy's largest telecommunications company, and has travelled the world.
But at home, he lets his mother wash his clothes, iron his shirts, tidy his room and cook him breakfast and dinner.
He is a "mammone" (mother's boy) and proud of it.
"We live well together. We're like roommates," he says.
Like many Italian men, Alessandro stayed at home for economic reasons when he was starting his career. But now he stays there because it is just too comfortable to leave.
The number of men in their 30s who still have not left the nest has increased in Italy in the last six years, according to recent figures by the national statistitcs institute Istat.
More than 60 percent of men between 25 and 29 and almost one-third between 30 and 34 live at home with their parents.
Meagre starting salaries that do not significantly rise in the early years of a career leave many no choice but to stay home rather than pay the high rents of most Italian cities.
"If I made twice my salary, I would have been able to move out a long time ago," said Marco, Alessandro's 29-year-old brother, who also lives at home with mamma.
"But leaving would mean barely being able to manage between rent and expenses," said Marco, who is an assistant professor of statistics at Rome's La Sapienza university.
MANY "MAMMONI" ARE UNEMPLOYED
Instead, with a monthly contribution for household expenses, both Alessandro and Marco live in a spacious, comfortable apartment in a prestigious Rome neighbourhood.
Many of Italy's "mammoni" are not even lucky enough to have a job. Unemployment, especially among the young, is in the 35 percent range and as high as 55 percent in the poorer south.

Parliament is preparing a bill to boost youth employment and shake up Italy's stodgy labour market. But it will be some time before legislation can improve economic conditions enough to convince "mammoni" to strike out on their own.
Today, rather than face Italy's bleak job market, many young men and women prefer to linger in the country's overcrowded and inefficient universities until their late 20s.
Even the eight percent of the Italian population between 24 and 35 who do graduate from university take at least two years to find employment. The most feasible option is to stay home.
But many sociologists believe the root of Italy's "mammismo" is much deeper than economics.
Italian mothers' boys admit they just like to be pampered.
"Why leave when there's someone who cooks my meals and irons my shirts," Alessandro said. "There's no real motivation. I live well here."
Alessandro owns an apartment the family bought in his name. But he prefers to keep it empty and live at home until he marries.

"Mammismo" has become such a common fact of life that a real estate magazine in Rome advertises with a poster picturing a 30-something man wearing a frilled white nightcap and bib and sucking a dummy.
"Still at home with mum?" the advert asks.
ARE MOTHERS' BOYS OUTSTAYING THEIR WELCOME?
More men stay at home than women, mainly because women marry earlier, according to the Istat study.
Rossana Palombo, an expert on family issues at the National Centre for Research, says staying home longer makes people more prepared for family life when they do marry.
"Whether it's the pasta or the ironed shirts, the Italian mother has been able to keep her sons at home. This is a great achievement of the Italian family," she says.
"And it doesn't in any way mean they are less mature. On the contrary, when they do start their own families they are much more attentive to values," she said.
Population experts say "mammismo" is one reason that Italy has one of the lowest birthrates in the world.
The Istat study even prompted editorialists normally concerned with politics to worry out loud about the long-term consequences of "mammismo" for Italy.

"Instead of choosing the outside world, life, and other cultures, our young people hide in the safety of the family cocoon. This is a sign of a society going backwards, not forwards," commented the newspaper La Repubblica.
Even some some mothers who admit to being over-protective -- including Alessandro's and Marco's -- are beginning to ask if their sons may be overstaying their welcome.
"In a selfish way, I'm happy because I like having them around. It keeps me feeling young. But by staying home, they give up leading their own lives," she said.
"I would never tell them to leave, but to tell the truth, I hope they do."
